questions.q: Why does a multi-source data warehouse migration usually default to a phased, parallel-run cutover instead of big-bang?
options: Big-bang has no partial-failure mode — an uncaught bug breaks everything for every consumer at once, while phased cutover lowers the blast radius
Phased cutover is always faster to complete than big-bang
Big-bang cutover is illegal for regulated data
Parallel-run requires no validation at all
questions.explain: Phased cutover moves consumers over one report at a time, so each validated move is evidence the migration works before the next one moves.

questions.q: What makes a reconciliation query actually useful during a parallel-run window?
options: It runs repeatedly across the whole window, diffing the same business question against both systems — not just checked once and trusted
It only needs to run a single time, right after cutover starts
It replaces the need for a rollback plan
It only checks row counts, never actual values
questions.explain: Zero rows returned, across the full parallel-run window, is the actual bar for calling a report validated — a single clean check isn't enough.

questions.q: What three questions must a rollback plan answer before cutover starts?
options: What's the trigger, what's the mechanism, and how long the old source stays alive
Who approved the migration budget, and when
What the new warehouse's table names are
How many rows the new warehouse contains
questions.explain: These have to be pre-agreed, not improvised during an incident — especially how long the old source is kept alive, since retiring it too early can't be undone.

questions.q: What decides whether a specific report is "go" for cutover?
options: Zero unexplained reconciliation variance for the full agreed window, plus the consumer confirming they can see the new warehouse
Whichever the migration team feels most confident about
The report having the most stakeholders
The report being the oldest one on the old system
questions.explain: This is a pre-agreed, objective bar — the same instinct as the freshness-SLA and incident-response thinking used earlier in the track.

questions.q: What's the single rollback-plan mistake this lesson calls out as unrecoverable?
options: Retiring the old source too early, before there's still something to roll back to
Running the reconciliation query too many times
Keeping the old source alive for too long
Documenting the rollback trigger in writing
questions.explain: Everything else in a rollback plan can be adjusted; retiring the fallback source removes the option to use it at all.
